item.title: Hello Robot, A&K Robotics to discuss how robots navigate crowded indoor spaces at RoboBusiness
item.dc:creator: The Robot Report Staff
item.description:
As robots move beyond warehouses and other controlled environments and into everyday life, navigation challenges will be critical.

The post Hello Robot, A&K Robotics to discuss how robots navigate crowded indoor spaces at RoboBusiness appeared first on The Robot Report.
item.ns3:encoded:
On the left, Hello Robot’s Stretch 4, and on the right, A&K Robotics’ Cruz autonomous pod. | Source: Hello Robot, A&K Robotics

Consumer-facing spaces are dynamic, crowded, and highly unpredictable, requiring robots to safely navigate around constantly changing obstacles, operate in diverse lighting conditions, navigate narrow passages and cluttered spaces, integrate with existing infrastructure, and balance autonomy with safety.

As robots move beyond warehouses and other controlled environments and into everyday life, solving these navigation challenges will be critical to achieving broad consumer acceptance and large-scale deployment.

At RoboBusiness 2026, Aaron Edsinger, the co-founder and CEO of Hello Robot, and Matt Anderson, the co-founder and CEO of A&K Robotics, will take part in the session, “Shared Spaces: Navigating Challenges for Indoor Robots.”

RoboBusiness will be on Oct. 20 and 21 in Santa Clara, Calif. Edsinger and Anderson will give their talk at 3:30 p.m. PT on the first day of the show in the Engineering Theater.

Meet the speakers

Aaron Edsinger is co-founder and CEO of Hello Robot, which developing practical, safe, and accessible robots for people. With a passion for building robots and robot companies, he has founded four companies focused on bringing human collaborative robots to the consumer, manufacturing, healthcare and research markets.

Two of these companies, Meka Robotics and Redwood Robotics, were acquired by Google in 2013. As robotics director at Google, Edsinger led the business, product and technical development of two of Google’s central investments in robotics, and worked closely with senior vice president and C-level executives to define the overall robotics strategy.

Edsinger is a recognized robotics innovator with a broad understanding of the entire robot product design stack, including human–robot interaction, UX design, and mechanical design. He is also an expert in design for manufacture, industrial design, software architecture, and real-time control, as well as design of force-controlled arms, actuators, hands and humanoids.

Matt Anderson is co-founder and CEO of A&K Robotics, which is building autonomous mobility infrastructure for complex, human-centered environments such as airports. He leads the company’s product strategy, which includes Cruz, a self-driving mobility robot that carries passengers through high-traffic, dynamic environments such as airport terminals, and Kineos AI, a platform for socially intelligent autonomy that enables systems to move naturally through dynamic spaces.

Anderson brings credibility with enterprise and public-sector partners by translating advanced autonomy into institution-ready solutions. He has over 10 years of experience building and bringing to market advanced technologies ranging from autonomous aerial drones to surgical devices.

Matt is an alumnus of Creative Destruction Lab’s AI and Machine Learning program. In a past life, he was a Chartered Accountant working in finance, investment, and business development.

item.title: Promise Robotics partners with D.R. Horton on physical AI for homebuilding
item.dc:creator: Eugene Demaitre
item.description:
Promise Robotics has signed a multi-year partnership with America's largest homebuilder by volume to bring physical AI to construction.

The post Promise Robotics partners with D.R. Horton on physical AI for homebuilding appeared first on The Robot Report.
item.ns3:encoded:
Promise Robotics says it can accelerate homebuilding by standardizing component manufacturing. Source: Promise Robotics

The construction industry is fragmented and has been relatively conservative about adopting new technologies, but physical AI promises to modernize homebuilding. Today, Promise Robotics said it has signed a multi-year agreement with D.R. Horton, which will use its Factory-as-a-Service capabilities to produce more than 1,250 homes in the U.S.

“Homebuilding has long lacked the production infrastructure needed to scale with the speed, predictability, and efficiency of modern manufacturing,” stated Ramtin Attar, co-founder and CEO of Promise Robotics. “Physical AI changes that by creating a new production model that can expand capacity within and across markets. Our goal is to make that capability accessible to builders across North America and support the industry’s long-term growth.”

“We started the company on the central thesis that robotics for the homebuilding space needed a very different approach and tech stack,” he told The Robot Report. “We started with mechanical and HVAC, and w’ve built the physical AI infrastructure for building component manufacturing.”

Founded in 2021, Promise Robotics said it has integrated robotics, AI, software, and manufacturing systems to connect the homebuilding workflow, from design translation and production planning through automated manufacturing and onsite installation. The Toronto-based company claimed that its Factory-as-a-Service (FaaS) model enables homebuilders to access advanced production infrastructure without the cost, complexity, or risk of developing and operating it themselves.

Construction needs to be more repeatable

As construction firms navigate persistent housing demand, labor shortages, rising costs, and pressure to increase output, they are searching for more repeatable and scalable ways to expand production, said Promise Robotics.

“Unlike traditional manufacturing, especially automotive, where there are five or six big players, the construction industry is large but fragmented,” explained Attar. “The workforce for homebuilding is also highly fragmented between businesses that manage the land, consumer houses, and seasonal trades. It doesn’t invest in the workforce in the same way as traditional manufacturing.”

“There’s no such thing as productization, in which the same car is built millions of times with small variations,” he added. “Even in the same home, every floor or wall is different. The clearances, components, and layouts are different.”

“To tackle this set of technical and business challenges, we take a distributed manufacturing approach,” said Attar. “Microfactories are a good problem for AI to solve, and we’ve spent years developing the foundational model and systems around construction.”

Software provides flexibility, scalability, says Promise Robotics

Promise Robotics handles that variability and resilience with software that can understand the limits of what’s possible, in terms of motion, building materials, and tools, Attar noted.

The company’s software can improve over time, allowing for reduced expenses. It is currently working with its own cloud-based simulations and KUKA industrial robot arms, but it is robot-agnostic, he said.

“We have a pretty deep tech stack, incorporating computer vision, LLMs [large language models] for initial prep of data flows, and a reasoning model that’s domain-specific,” said Attar. “For every home we build, we produce 300 new images, 5,000 new tactile sources, and a lot of processes. We’re very data rich, and that’s why we present ourselves as a physical AI infrastructure and not just a technology.”

“Our floors are 45 ft. and walls are 20 ft.,” he explained. “The walls have windows and doors in them. We’re also manufacturing stair cages that can be dropped in for fast assembly. Our sweet spot is townhomes between three to four stories. Taller than that, and there’s more need for sprinklers, bracing, and metalwork.”

The company can build a two-family home with two stories, a basement, and a garage in one day, not including electronics, window installations, and plumbing. That process typically takes two to three weeks, Attar said.

Promise Robotics integrates construction workflows with FaaS

Promise Robotics said its technology interprets existing home designs, generates production plans and robotic instructions, orchestrates manufacturing, and connects that production with site installation. Rather than automating isolated tasks, the company said it brings these capabilities together in one integrated environment.

“FaaS gives a broad range of homebuilders across geographies access to an integrated production platform,” said Promise Robotics. The FaaS model can help builders improve cycle times, increase capacity, and scale more predictably across communities and markets, it added.

“While every house we build is different, the process is the same — handling files, translating them into robotic instructions,” Attar said. “The robots are trained to build with highly variable components. We need to be able to support a lot of different types of builders and different types of products. We’re building everything from single to multiple units to duplexes and fourplexes, townhomes, so forth. And it’s never the same.”

Promise Robotics is setting up its initial FaaS facilities in Edmonton and Calgary in Canada and Phoenix. Its own crews operate the systems for a tight feedback loop, Attar said.

Promise Robotics’ core technology includes fastening algorithms and can be set to comply with local building codes on things like spacing. “Unlike the harsh environment in Canada, Phoenix required 50% less  sheeting and different bracing,” said Attar. “Our system is built to adjust to different markets and generalize through AI.”

Promise Robotics is starting its Factory-as-a-Service in three North American cities. Source: Promise Robotics

D.R. Horton to help automation scale to U.S. market

The company noted that The U.S. market represents the largest opportunity to apply its model at scale. D.R. Horton, America’s largest homebuilder by volume, is the first major U.S. homebuilder to use Promise Robotics’ platform.

“At D.R. Horton, we are always looking for innovations that can help us improve how we build. We are continuously focused on improving cycle times, increasing production capacity, and bringing greater consistency and predictability to our operations,” said Brad Conlon, senior vice president for strategic growth and innovation at D.R. Horton. “Promise Robotics’ integrated platform gives us a new capability to support those goals.”

“This is just the tarting point,” said Attar. “We need to earn the trust of each customer and really execute. We value the customers that take a leap with us, but with every home builder, we say, ‘You can buy as much capacity as you like,’ and we provide them with a journey to scale that across many parts of the market.”

Promise Robotics is not a vertically integrated developer or a home designer like Reframe Systems, Attar acknowledged. “We’re more about the advancements in robotics, and we’re here to scale when companies need to scale,” he said.

item.title: Closing the reality gap: Why real-time execution has become the new competitive advantage
item.dc:creator: Cecile Dick-Calmes
item.description:
Daifuku's Cecile Dick-Calmes said success is no longer measured solely by automation density or equipment utilization.

The post Closing the reality gap: Why real-time execution has become the new competitive advantage appeared first on The Robot Report.
item.ns3:encoded:
Daifuku helped to automate Kagetsudo Co.’s product storage system and production lines. | Source: Daifuku

Organizations across the supply chain continue to invest heavily in automation. Yet for many warehouse and distribution leaders, the expected gains in productivity, throughput, and agility remain elusive.

The issue is rarely a lack of technology. More often, it is a lack of synchronization.

As fulfillment networks become increasingly complex, a new challenge has emerged: the growing gap between what digital systems believe is happening and what is actually occurring on the warehouse floor. This disconnect, which can be described as the “reality gap,” is becoming one of the most significant barriers to operational performance.

Closing that gap is quickly becoming a defining capability for high-performing operations.

The new operational challenge: When digital and physical reality diverge

Modern warehouses generate enormous volumes of data. Inventory transactions, equipment status updates, labor activities, transportation events, and order flows are all captured and processed by various systems.

Yet data alone does not guarantee operational awareness.

In many facilities, information arrives too late, remains trapped in silos, or lacks the context needed to support timely decisions. As a result, operational leaders are often responding to events that have already occurred rather than actively managing conditions as they unfold.

The consequences are familiar:

  • Inventory records that do not accurately reflect physical reality
  • Congestion that develops before being detected
  • Bottlenecks that spread through interconnected processes
  • Labor and equipment deployed based on outdated conditions
  • Delays that compound across the fulfillment network

The reality gap is not simply a technology problem. It is an execution problem.

Why automation alone is no longer enough

For decades, the primary objective of warehouse automation was straightforward: reduce manual handling and improve efficiency within individual processes.

That approach delivered significant gains.

Today, however, automation environments are substantially more sophisticated. Facilities often operate multiple automated subsystems simultaneously, each capable of performing its intended function effectively. The challenge is ensuring those systems collectively support broader operational objectives.

A warehouse may have advanced automation, sophisticated software, and highly optimized processes. Yet if these elements are not continuously aligned around current operating conditions, inefficiencies remain.

This is why leading organizations are shifting their focus from automation itself to orchestration.

Automation enables movement. Orchestration enables performance. The distinction is becoming increasingly important as supply chains face greater volatility, labor constraints, and demands for faster fulfillment.

The rise of real-time execution

Closing the reality gap requires organizations to move beyond periodic visibility and toward real-time execution. Real-time execution is the ability to continuously sense operational conditions, evaluate changing circumstances, and coordinate responses across people, processes, and technology.

Rather than relying on static plans, organizations can dynamically adapt to what is actually occurring in the facility at any given moment.

This capability rests on several foundational principles:

  • Continuous awareness of operational conditions
  • Immediate detection of exceptions and disruptions
  • Dynamic allocation of work and resources
  • Rapid adaptation to changing demand and workloads
  • Coordinated decision-making across interconnected systems

The objective is not simply faster data collection. The objective is faster, better decisions. In increasingly complex fulfillment environments, decision speed is becoming as important as processing speed.

From connected operations to intelligent operations

Many organizations have spent the past decade focused on connectivity, integrating systems, collecting data, and creating visibility.

The next stage of operational maturity is intelligence.

The most effective operations are not necessarily those with the largest volume of data. They are the ones that can translate operational signals into action before small issues become significant disruptions.

This shift is changing how leaders think about operational performance.

Success is no longer measured solely by automation density or equipment utilization. Increasingly, it is measured by how effectively an organization can detect change, make decisions, and execute those decisions in real time. In other words, competitive advantage is migrating from assets to agility.

The strategic benefits of closing the reality gap

Organizations that successfully close the reality gap typically see benefits that extend well beyond efficiency gains.

They become more resilient when disruptions occur. They improve consistency and service quality because decisions are based on current conditions rather than historical assumptions. They create better utilization of resources by balancing workloads more effectively. They reduce operational friction that often leads to excessive labor demands, equipment bottlenecks, and inventory discrepancies.

Most importantly, they build operations capable of adapting continuously rather than reacting after the fact.

In an environment where customer expectations, labor availability, and market conditions are constantly changing, adaptability has become one of the most valuable operational capabilities an organization can develop.

Register now and help us celebrate 20 years of RoboBusiness!

Looking ahead

The future of warehouse performance will not be defined solely by the adoption of automation technologies. It will be defined by how effectively organizations connect planning with execution and digital intelligence with physical operations.

As facilities become more automated and supply chains grow more complex, the ability to maintain alignment between operational reality and system awareness will become increasingly critical.

The question for supply chain leaders is no longer whether automation is necessary. Now, the question is whether their organization can turn automation into coordinated, real-time execution.

Because in modern fulfillment operations, the greatest inefficiencies often exist not in the movement of products, but in the gap between knowing what is happening and acting on it.

About the author

Cecile Dick-Calmes is a content marketing strategist and creative leader with experience in B2B and B2C digital marketing. She is currently the inbound marketing manager at Daifuku Wynright and previously worked at The Boeing Co. as a community manager and at Hainan Airlines as the digital marketing lead.

item.title: Will ‘boring’ robots win in the real world? Why robotic form should follow workflow
item.dc:creator: Ron Zukerman
item.description:
If we want to move physical AI from social media feeds to a sustained commercial level, we must reverse our current approach.

The post Will ‘boring’ robots win in the real world? Why robotic form should follow workflow appeared first on The Robot Report.
item.ns3:encoded:
The Atlas humanoid robot doing a cartwheel. | Source: Boston Dynamics

Robots have captured our imagination. We have seen humanoids balancing on one leg, doing backflips, folding laundry, and moving smoothly over difficult terrain. This is all behavior that only a few years ago seemed like something out of science fiction. These viral examples matter because they show that embodied AI has reached a new technical stage.

At the same time, the window on what qualifies as a “humanoid robot” seems to be shifting. Robot companies are adding wheels, more sensors, new manipulators, hats, and screens, while they take away eyes and heads from their humanoid robot designs.

As an engineering ecosystem working directly alongside humanoid developers to solve core hardware bottlenecks, we see a recurring theme. The industry frequently gets caught up in “robot-forward” thinking. We build an extraordinary physical platform first, then scour industrial sites for a task for it to perform.

If we want to move physical AI from social media feeds to a sustained commercial level, we must reverse our current approach. The industry needs a design method that works backwards from the workflow. Begin with a task that has economic value. Consider whether a robot can carry out that task better than a human can.

Then, go backwards to find out exactly what hardware, sensing capabilities, and form factor are actually needed to carry out the task.

The sensor stack is born in the task, not the datasheet

Successful industrial robot forms follow their functions. Source: Vishay Precision Group Inc.

If you start by designing a platform, you will likely end up with a compromised hardware stack. The specific workflow determines the machine’s engineering requirements.

Let’s take as an example a bipedal humanoid robot that is asked to carry out two different industrial work processes. One involves inserting a pin on an automotive assembly line and the other involves packing a pallet in a logistics center.

A pin connector insertion task generally involves a 20 µm clearance and 5 N mating force. So, there needs to be contact-force resolution below 0.1 N and a control bandwidth fast enough to detect jamming before a sensitive pin bends.

Yet, when using the same arm for bulk pallet packing, you need almost none of that high-frequency micro-force resolution. Instead, you need heavy payload capacity, structural rigidity, and the ability to endure 1 million cycles without baseline mechanical drift.

If you are building a general-purpose platform, a single “middle-of-the-road” force sensor may result in a system that could make precise pin insertion difficult. The system could also lack the durability needed for continuous heavy lifting.

The workflow also determines your error budget. This is the only factor that turns force sensing from a cost item into something that provides a demonstrable return on investment.

Attempts to improve force sensing often fail. For example, our tests have shown that using a specific calculation maintaining contact force at ±0.2 N, can reduce connector scrap in amounts from 1.2% to 0.5%. This can translate into annual estimated savings of approximately $450,000 per assembly line. This kind of economic argument is only possible if you begin with the task in question.

That is exactly the reason why the selection of critical components, for example those based on strain sensing, must take place at the architectural design stage rather than being treated as an afterthought when preparing the bill of materials (BOM).

Strain sensing can provide valuable data if incorporated early in designs. Source: Vishay Precision Group

Adjusting the robot rather than adjusting the facility

The tendency to focus on the task first raises the main question about form factor. Is a specialised form factor the better choice? When is a humanoid design strictly necessary?

Operating environments can be divided into two types: greenfield and brownfield. The real issue is not what the robot should look like, but whether it is cheaper to modify the robot or to modify the facility.

With greenfield sites, you can use specialized robots. With brownfield sites, like an existing refinery or chemical plant, the robot has to adapt to spaces created for humans.

In greenfield builds, like Equinor’s Northern Lights facility, the operator can design the layout from the beginning and construct the facility around the task. So, specialized, non-humanoid forms almost always prove better in terms of unit economics, speed, and energy efficiency. Legged and wheeled robots are more reliable for the types of tasks they carry out.

However, in most cases, industrial activities take place in brownfield sites, where the only practical option is to adapt the existing platform. These sites have narrow aisles, stairs, floor grating, and doorways designed with the human body in mind. In this situation, a human-suitable form factor, whether that involves legs, two arms, or a humanoid shape, becomes a major advantage. It lets the equipment operate in environments designed for people without spending millions of dollars retrofitting the facilities.

The true test for a humanoid design is whether, if you were starting again, you would still go with a humanoid. When human compatibility is needed, the basic physical requirements stay the same: foot contact, joint torque, and wrist force.

The robots may come in different shapes, but they have the same sensory physics. Strain-based sensing endures even when the form factor changes, offering fundamental ground-truth measurement regardless of how your physical platform develops.

One test for humanoids is whether human compatibility is required. Source: Vishay Precision Group

Deployment depth beats demo breadth

Flashy viral videos show what is technically possible. The true test, however, is not the demonstration itself but the second purchase order. Only through repeat orders can business utility be proven.

Although demonstrations using units calibrated under climate-controlled conditions prove a robot can function once, full fleet deployment demands that the robot survive at least 10,000 cycles per shift amid constant thermal variation and with near-zero tolerance for drift.

Most physical AI projects fail because the engineering effort turns instead to broad, general promises before addressing specific operational facts. In real-world situations, deployments fail due to drift, sensor fatigue, and recalibration challenges, not flaws in reasoning.

Editor’s note: Humanoids and physical AI are among the session track topics at RoboBusiness 2026, which will be on Oct. 20 and 21 in Santa Clara, Calif. Register now to attend.

Register now and help us celebrate 20 years of RoboBusiness!

The physical AI balance sheet

Integrating AI into physical hardware requires a disciplined balance between power consumption, thermal dissipation, mechanical wear, and safety limitations. With software, you scale by making copies; with hardware, you have to buy it, build it, and wait.

Teams that take a software approach often fail to account for this physical balance sheet. Beyond basic thermal or electrical limits, non-linear actuator gear reductions introduce complex behaviour that is notoriously difficult to predict and simulate.

True backdrivability solves part of this problem by allowing the robot actuator or joint to fully reflect any physical impact from the environment back to the core control architecture.

Whatever the hardware bottleneck may be, whether it’s thermal throttling in the joint actuators or the amount of power drawn under peak load, each constraint comes down to the same need: knowing exactly what force is present under actual loading conditions, at real temperatures, over a period of years. This is the information that strain-based sensing provides, which is why it should be included in the architecture and not just listed in the bill of materials.

Robot safety requires more than software, according to Vishay Precision Group. Source: ANYbotics

The real metrics of commercial viability

To assess the commercial viability of physical AI systems, we should go beyond slick-looking marketing videos. Instead, we should focus on the metrics that finance teams actually care about.

The most important and essential metric is mean time between interventions (MTBI). This can be considered the most genuine measure used in the industry, but is the one that is least often published. If a human operator has to intervene every 20 minutes to unjam a gripper or reset a drifted sensor, then high autonomy figures have little significance.

We need to assign the same importance to the actual cost per unit of work, whether calculated on a per-pick, per meter travelled, or per inspection completed basis. This figure ultimately determines whether a robot fleet will replace or augment existing labour.

Operational value also depends on redeployment time. Deployment time shows whether a “general-purpose” platform can swiftly adjust to a new task or whether reconfiguration requires weeks of custom engineering. Lastly, the number of safety incidents per operating hour will determine if the robot ever goes outside of its cage to operate freely among human workers.

A viral video shows a robot capable of carrying out a given task once. However, a sustainable business needs the robot to carry out that same task at least 10,000 times in a row, without any intervention, drift, or failure.

The main conclusion is straightforward: Start with the workflow, build reliable sensing into the core architecture, and focus on operational metrics so both specialised machines and humanoid platforms can fulfil their potential in the physical world.

About the author

Ron Zukerman is an innovation director at Vishay Precision Group Inc. (VPG). The company is a leader in precision measurement and sensing technologies.

VPG said its sensors, weighing solutions and measurement systems optimize and enhance customers’ product performance across a broad array of markets to make the world safer, smarter, and more productive. To learn more, visit the company at www.vpgsensors.com and follow it on LinkedIn.

item.title: Why dexterity is physical AI’s real bottleneck
item.dc:creator: Nicolas Sauvage
item.description:
The next major challenge in robotic dexterity is making the entire system reliable enough to turn capabilities into useful work.

The post Why dexterity is physical AI’s real bottleneck appeared first on The Robot Report.
item.ns3:encoded:
Nicolas Sauvage, founder and president of TDK Ventures, with ANYbotics’ quadruped robot. | Source: TDK Ventures

A robot picks up an object, moves it, and puts it down successfully. Is it dexterous? Perhaps. But now ask it to do that successfully hundreds of times, while objects move slightly, its grip changes, components wear, and unexpected failures occur. That is a much harder test of dexterity, and a much better measure of whether a robot is dexterous enough for the real world.

We are making rapid progress in what robots can manipulate. However, useful dexterity isn’t simply the ability to complete an individual action once. It is the ability to sense, grasp, move, adjust and recover reliably enough to complete an entire workflow without constant human assistance.

A robot that succeeds 99% of the time sounds ready for work, but a job rarely consists of a single action. Consider a workflow that requires 100 physical actions in a sequence. At a 99% success rate for each action, the probability that all 100 succeed on the first attempt is just 36.6%. Increase the success rate to 99.9%, and the probability of completing the workflow rises to 90.5%. At 99.99%, it reaches 99.0%.

This is, of course, a simplified example that assumes equal and independent success rates, but it illustrates an important point. A robot with a 99% success rate is not necessarily 99% automated.

Small reliability gaps become much bigger when repeated across an entire workflow. This means that a robot that looks almost flawless in a demonstration can still be far from ready for autonomous deployment. The difference between two nines and four nines may ultimately decide whether a robot is ready to work alone.

The next major challenge in robotic dexterity is not simply teaching robots to do more, but making the entire system reliable enough to turn those capabilities into useful work.

Dexterity is a system, not a hand

Robotic dexterity is often discussed as a hardware race: more fingers, more joints and more freedom of movement. While those capabilities obviously matter, the customer does not buy degrees of freedom. The customer buys useful work.

Completing that work requires a closed loop across vision, position, contact, force, pressure, grasp, movement, and adjustment. Power, safety, flexibility, and recovery also matter.

Not every workflow needs touch, as in some cases, vision and movement data may provide enough information. But touch can also be useful in telling a robot that an object is slipping, the contact is unstable, too much pressure is being applied, or a component is properly in place.

The objective therefore isn’t to pile every sense onto every robot, but to give the system enough of the right information to act, and recover, reliably.

TDK Ventures helps early-stage materials, energy, cleantech, industry 5.0, mobility, and health tech startups scale. | Source: TDK Ventures

More nines come from learning

Recovery is a huge part of dexterity. If a robot begins to lose its grip on an object, the useful measure isn’t if the original grasp was perfect; it’s whether the system can detect the slip early enough to correct it before a small error causes the entire task to fail.

A failure discovered during deployment might expose a problem in software, sensing, or control, or it might reveal that the hardware itself needs redesigning. Changing the hand changes movement, sensing and calibration, so data collected with one physical design may not transfer directly to another. Real-world deployment is therefore a critical part of the development process.

Deployment reveals slips, poor grasps, wear, and failed recoveries. Those experiences become data that can improve software, simulation, sensing, control, and hardware. Each cycle can make the next deployment more reliable and less expensive.

A technological breakthrough may begin the journey, but it is the learning system around it that multiplies its impact. Robotic dexterity should be viewed in much the same way. Additional nines emerge from repeatedly deploying, learning and improving.

Editor’s note: Physical AI, enabling technologies, and humanoids are among the session track topics at RoboBusiness 2026, which will be on Oct. 20 and 21 in Santa Clara, Calif. Register now to attend.

Register now and help us celebrate 20 years of RoboBusiness!

The right body depends on the work

Reliability also requires us to resist the temptation to equate more human-like robots with better robots. The starting point should be the job. From there, work backwards to determine the environment, physical form, and system required to perform it.

Dexterity should follow the same logic. The most human-like hand may not be the best hand for a particular workflow. The goal is not maximum dexterity. It is the minimum sufficient dexterity needed to complete valuable work reliably, and we are already starting to see this principle being successfully deployed.

Agility‘s Digit is a bipedal robot designed for logistics and industrial work. Digit can connect directly to specialized tools suited to the job, rather than requiring a five-fingered hand or being made to look as human-like as possible. It has the form and dexterity the work actually requires.

ANYbotics applies the same principle to a different environment. Its four-legged robots can navigate stairs and uneven surfaces at industrial sites, while inspecting hazardous areas reduces the need for human exposure. In one deployment, its technology has reportedly carried out more than 33,000 inspections across 450 inspection points.

Starship Technologies takes a different approach. Its delivery robots need to travel along pavements, so a small, wheeled form is better suited to the job than legs. That purpose-built approach has helped Starship to report more than 10 million autonomous deliveries.

These robots look and operate very differently because they perform very different jobs. Yet they demonstrate the same principle: The right physical form is the one that fits the work and can perform it repeatedly in the real environment.

Our investments in Agility, ANYbotics, and Starship have changed the questions I ask as an investor, particularly during our ongoing deep exploration into dexterity. I am less interested in which robot looks most human than in which complete system can reach the reliability its customer actually requires.

Sauvage with Agility Robotics’ Digit humanoid robot. | Source: TDK Ventures

Measure the job, not the demonstration

This changes how we should measure progress in physical AI. The success rate of an individual action shown in a demonstration tells us very little about whether a robot is actually ready to work autonomously in the real world.

I want to know what percentage of complete workflows finish without human assistance. When something goes wrong, how often can the robot recover without help? How does performance change when the object, lighting, position, wear or surrounding environment changes?

Then there are the less glamorous questions that become extremely important at scale. What breaks first under repeated use? How quickly can it be diagnosed, repaired and returned to work? What are the speed, uptime, and cost of each successfully completed job?

These are ultimately better measures of dexterity than what a robot can demonstrate once. A robot does not need the most human-like hand, the greatest number of joints or the widest possible range of skills to create value. It needs the right combination of physical form, sensing, control, and recovery to complete a valuable job reliably in the environment where it will actually work.

That is where I believe the next phase of progress in robotic dexterity will be won. The industry has made extraordinary advances in what robots are capable of doing. Now the challenge is turning those capabilities into systems that customers can trust to perform useful work repeatedly, recover when something goes wrong, and improve through deployment.

About the author

Nicolas Sauvage is the founder and president of TDK Ventures, the global corporate venture capital arm of TDK Corp. He launched the firm in 2019 around a simple principle: entrepreneurs come first.

Today, TDK Ventures manages $500 million across four funds and backs early-stage startups globally, across AI and compute, energy, industrial and robotics, mobility, and advanced materials.

item.title: Boston Dynamics gives more insight into its redesigned humanoid hand
item.dc:creator: Brianna Wessling
item.description:
The Robot Report spoke with Alberto Rodriguez, the director of robot behavior for Atlas at Boston Dynamics, about the humanoid's new hand.

The post Boston Dynamics gives more insight into its redesigned humanoid hand appeared first on The Robot Report.
item.ns3:encoded:
Boston Dynamics said its new hand is still capable of handling over 100 lb. | Source: Boston Dynamics

Last week, Boston Dynamics Inc. gave a look at its new humanoid robot hand. The four-fingered hand has 13 degrees of freedom, or DoF, and is directly actuated. The company said it designed it for mass manufacturing.

Lots of things immediately stand out about the hand. Notably, Boston Dynamics has dropped the pinky finger and reduced the size of the gripper. Less obviously, the company said it built the new hand for high-fidelity simulation to enable sim-to-real reinforcement learning (RL).

To learn more about the new hand, The Robot Report spoke with Alberto Rodriguez, the director of robot behavior for Atlas at Boston Dynamics.

What did Boston Dynamics learn from its humanoid trials that it applied to the new hand?

Rodriguez: Having a product roadmap for Atlas has been a key enabler when it came to making hard decisions like what is the right level of complexity that we should be packing into a hand and navigating its design tradeoff between dexterity, strength, ruggedness, cost, reparability, and sensing.

We have learned things from the design of Atlas’ body. There are things like simplicity, modularity, and actuator maturity that make sense in theory, but over time, you start appreciating the huge impact they have in the velocity you can move.

A reliable robot allows you to capture data faster, run more experiments, and take bets at early deployments. Modularity allows you to focus with more energy on a smaller number of things that you need to get right. That also allows you to move faster.

We have used the same philosophy with this hand. It is built out of 13 identical actuators, all completely encapsulated, with no fragile cables crossing joints, which is already paying off.

We have also learned, for example, that the earlier hands were strong enough to lift 100 lb.-plus heavy objects, so we did not need to increase strength, and we could consider decreasing it a bit to further improve actuation transparency. We also experienced the challenges that earlier hands had with certain more complex tasks, which have influenced the current design.  

Did you look at any off-the-shelf end effectors, and why did you decide to build a hand in-house?

Rodriguez: We always look at what is out there to understand the state-of-the-art. Hands are a key piece of technology that are so integral to the value proposition of humanoids that it would be very difficult for us to approach it in any other way than in-house.

As we described in our blog post, all hands come out of a very consequential tradeoff of capabilities, and understanding how it fits into the product roadmap is key.

How does Boston Dynamics ensure durability so the gripper can last through many shifts?

Rodriguez: This isn’t much different from how we do it for other key technologies in the robot.

It all starts from an amazing hardware design team that has done this many times before and has built intuition for what leads to reliable hardware.

We also have a strong culture of collaboration between the behavior and hardware teams in those early design phases to lock in key design features, like morphology, sensing, torque distribution, etc., by using techniques like simulation or mockup designs. This allows the hardware team to go into the detailed design with more confidence.

We build early prototypes and put them in the hands of the systems, controls, and behavior teams for a while to unearth as many as possible of the unknown unknowns and iterate on the design.

Then, we put the hands and various subcomponents through their paces under rigorous validation and verification tests to check that their behavior is at par with expectations. While this is tedious and might initially slow down the deployment of new hardware, it ends up speeding up the process by allowing to refine issues faster than having to painfully discover them in the field.

What kinds of tasks have you been testing with the new hand?

Rodriguez: All kinds. It is difficult to define requirements on a system as complex as a hand, and one way to do it is to build a suite of representative tasks of what the hand is meant to do in the future. Many of these are common industrial tasks like using handheld power tools, handling cables, and fishing for screws.

We have also used these hands on many tasks that are less mission-oriented, such as bring-up tasks that we use to compare against earlier hands, and in other tasks that help us explore the limits of what the hands are capable of.

As always, we like taking inspiration from feats of human physical achievement — such as parkour or gymnastics — to push ourselves and do it in a way that connects with people. We have been playing with different types of juggling and speed hand games.

Boston Dynamics said it didn’t set out to build a complicated hand, but instead a reliable one capable of using tools. | Source: Boston Dynamics

Can you tell us more about Boston Dynamics process deciding how many fingers to include on the hand?

Rodriguez: The process relies on intuition, periods of large entropy in concept designs, and then a suite of tasks or behaviors that we wanted the hand to be able to do. Our product roadmap gives us concrete manipulation tasks that we know are in scope for Atlas.

Tool use is an important example, but there are many more, from how small are the screws that Atlas should be able to pick to how small are the spaces where Atlas should be able to put its hands in.

Another useful way to scope hand requirements is as a set of motions that are important for dexterous manipulative behavior, and measure designs against them. Here are some of the key motions that we focused on:

  • Being able to slide the fingertip of the thumb along the lengths of the other fingers
  • Being able to slide the fingertip of the thumb across the fingers
  • Being able to rock the fingertip of the thumb against the index finger in a dexterous pinch grasp
  • Being able to exert power grasps on triggered tool handles

Decisions like the number of fingers or the number of joints per finger are difficult, but we try to keep a pragmatic perspective and a clear line of sight to factors like cost and reliability that are key to be able to scale manufacturing.

For example, a design that had a lot of initial support was a hand with two thumbs, one on each side. This design had the added benefit that you do not need to have two separate right and left hands. You can make them on a single assembly line.

We finally decided against it because it involves extra actuation complexity that ultimately incurred extra DoFs, cost, and volume.

What about the hand makes it easier to work with in simulation and for reinforcement learning?

Rodriguez: We design the actuation and transmission with an eye to backdrivability and transparency. On the controls side, we have developed techniques to compensate for some of the remaining non-idealities on the actuators, like compensating for different types of friction.

All of this enables accurate dynamic simulation, key for the design philosophy of the entire robot. This makes reinforcement learning more effective at training policies that can use proprioception, where the actuators themselves sense that you are pushing back on them and transfer directly to hardware.

This is the exact same recipe that has succeeded for agile humanoid behavior in the past few years. Build actuators that simulate well, and then rely on RL at scale.

I am convinced that the ability to use RL in simulation is going to be a key enabler for the next generation of manipulation capabilities for complex dexterity, going beyond pick and place. These are tasks that are difficult to teleoperate or demonstrate, because a lot of the relevant information to reproduce them is in the quick changes of the distribution of contacts and pressure.

Have you started testing the hand at RMAC, and what have the results been so far?

Rodriguez: Not yet. We have used the new hands extensively in our headquarters but have not deployed them yet to the whole robot fleet. That is a process that requires coordination and time to make sure that it does not disrupt regular operations like data collection or applications.

item.title: Groceryshop 2026 shows that retail robots are ready to scale, use AI
item.dc:creator: Georges Mirza
item.description:
Groceryshop 2026 not only featured mobile robots for taking inventory, but it also showed how retail automation is evolving.

The post Groceryshop 2026 shows that retail robots are ready to scale, use AI appeared first on The Robot Report.
item.ns3:encoded:
Groceryshop 2026 provided an opportunity to assess the state of retail robotics. Source: Georges Mirza

It has been more than a decade since I first helped to bring robots to live retail center stores. Long gone are retailers’ concerns about robots taking jobs, scaring kids, accidentally bumping into shoppers, or simply disrupting the grocery shopping experience.

It is good to see how much the industry has advanced; we have come a long way. Now that we are seeing scale, we can start using near-real-time shelf insights across more retail solutions. In this AI age of disruption, there is no excuse for not prioritizing and benefiting from these insights.

Is the broader retail solution space ready to advance and make this data actionable? I attended Groceryshop 2026 last month to find out.

Simbe continues to scale with Tally robot

The major announcement came from Simbe Robotics, which has now completed the rollout of 3,000 Tally robots globally across retailers and countries. With an ongoing rollout at a Tier 1 retailer, that number will quickly grow, marking another major accomplishment for robotics in retail.

Simbe has also been proactive in building capabilities to make its data actionable, from analytics dashboards to virtual store tours. That proactive approach will be critical to staying relevant as the retail technology environment continues to evolve.

How far can Simbe go on its own in developing these capabilities before it begins to overlap with established solutions? And how quickly will those established solutions begin consuming this new source of shelf data? A new way of thinking is certainly needed across the industry. It remains to be seen whether this disruption will trigger the change that is needed.

Badger Technologies builds a retail intelligence layer

Badger Technologies appears to be making a similar transition. In my discussion with its newly appointed CEO, John Gehre, at Groceryshop, he described Badger as evolving from a robotics company into a retail intelligence company.

The robot remains the platform for capturing shelf and store data, but the focus is shifting toward making that information actionable, down to how it can improve decisions and execution at the individual store level.

Moving beyond the basics of identifying out-of-stocks and price tags, Badger is exploring whether the continuous data collected as the robot moves through the aisle can be applied to estimate how much product remains on the shelf, when replenishment is needed, and when it will reach peak freshness.

The company continues to stand out with its multifunctional robotic platform, as well as the engineering and manufacturing scale of Jabil behind it. The question is whether it can now leverage those advantages to move faster.

ShelfOptix rethinks the deployment model

ShelfOptix is taking a somewhat different approach to scaling retail robotics. While continuing to strengthen its computer vision and actionable shelf intelligence powered by BrainOS, the more interesting differentiator may be its deployment model.

The company is targeting smaller-format retailers, including drug, convenience, dollar, and regional grocery, with a foldable robot that can travel between stores escorted by a human rather than remain permanently deployed in one location.

That model lowers the hurdle of dedicating a robot to every store and opens the door to recurring audits across a broader footprint. It is a practical approach to matching the economics of robotics to the needs of different retail formats.

Blue Collar Robotics picks up the retail slack

Newcomer Blue Collar Robotics participated in the startup pitch and was selected as a finalist. The company is taking on a harder but potentially more transformative retail use case: physically picking products in the store.

Rather than focusing on shelf scanning, the startup is developing a mobile robot designed to move products between shelves and carts, with initial customer trials planned as it works toward commercialization. The challenge is significant, requiring navigation, vision, picking, controls, and back-end integration to work together reliably.

This is ultimately what I believe will be the long-term role for robots in retail stores: moving from observing retail execution to actually performing it. It is an exponentially more difficult use case that the industry is beginning to pursue, and it will take time to mature before robots can deliver accurately, repeatedly, at scale, and with speed.

MUSE expands modular approach to retail

MUSE, last year’s Shark Reef Startup Pitch winner, was back at Groceryshop continuing to expand the capabilities of its modular robotic platform. The robot moves product through the store, allowing store labor to focus on restocking.

The company has added modules to guide customers to item locations and support in-store promotions. It is also developing additional modules for picking and replenishment, security, and floor cleaning.

With additional funding and a pilot underway with a small U.S. store chain, MUSE is looking to grow and gain a stronger foothold in the U.S. market. It is a very aggressive and wide-ranging approach to expanding the robot’s capabilities.

I will be watching how the company takes what it learns from deployments, along with recent technology advances, to deliver against an equally aggressive roadmap.

The path toward end-to-end shelf automation

As robots become increasingly capable of continuously collecting pricing, inventory, RFID, and visual data, simply delivering another data feed or API is no longer enough. The next competitive battleground will be how effectively that intelligence is translated into actions that improve store execution.

This will accelerate as legacy solutions begin to ingest this data. I still believe many of these decade-old systems will become far more relevant when they start consuming actual shelf conditions instead of relying on plan data, random compliance checks, and point-of-sale data without a true understanding of the retail real estate that generated the sale.

That will be a major step toward end-to-end shelf automation. It will make some existing shelf solutions obsolete – a welcome outcome – and make others far more relevant.

The future is here, more so than ever. What an era to be living through and observing, as innovation begins to deliver accurately, repeatedly, at scale, and with speed – at a velocity still unfamiliar to this industry.

About the author

Georges Mirza has been at the forefront of retail and consumer packaged goods (CPG) innovation, building market-leading category management and retail analytics solutions that achieved majority market share. He pioneered advancements in robotic data collection and image recognition, addressing challenges like out-of-stocks and inventory accuracy.

Today, Mirza advises and collaborates with retail and technology leaders to shape and scale next-generation growth strategies. Follow him on LinkedIn or X.

item.title: SafeWorld emerges from stealth to build, deploy robot safety simulation technologies
item.dc:creator: Brianna Wessling
item.description:
SafeWorld’s platform provides testing and simulation software to help enterprises evaluate and deploy robots safely and responsibly.

The post SafeWorld emerges from stealth to build, deploy robot safety simulation technologies appeared first on The Robot Report.
item.ns3:encoded:
SafeWorld said its platform can work in a range of industries with a range of robot embodiments, including robots arms, humanoids, mobile robots, and more. | Source: SafeWorld

SafeWorld this week emerged from stealth with $12.2 million in seed funding. The startup aims to make safety testing on AI-powered robots easier with its simulation technology.

“Our point of view is that if you’re going to have more capable robots, it just makes sense that you need to have more capable ways to test and to validate those robots,” Kyle Wong, co-founder and CEO of SafeWorld, told The Robot Report. “Otherwise, you’re not going to deploy those robots.”

“We already have been using robots for maybe 100 years,” said Ding Zhao, co-founder of SafeWorld and director of the Safe AI Lab at Carnegie Mellon University. “We started the company today because, when AI came, it actually brought automation to the next level. The robots, for the first time, were allowed to go out of the cage and share the same space with humans.”

Zhao asserted that this level of collaboration requires a whole new level of understanding for the robot, which is where SafeWorld comes in.

Shine Capital and a16z Speedrun co-led the funding round. It also included participation from Box Group, Carnegie Mellon University Endowment, Innovation Endeavors, SV Angel, and other leading venture capitalists and angel investors.

Ultimately, SafeWorld wants to make it easier for robotics companies to build safe systems. The Oakland, Calif.-based company currently has customers in industrial, manufacturing, logistics, construction, and even some home use cases, Wong said.

“Robotics companies themselves need to, of course, be accountable for safety,” said Wong. “The question, though, is more, ‘Should they build it from scratch every single time?’ We don’t think that makes sense.”

Inside SafeWorld’s platform

SafeWorld said it gives enterprises a scalable way to test how robots behave around people in rare, dangerous, and unexpected situations, without putting anyone at risk.

“These are safety scenarios that have not existed yet in the world,” Wong said. “So then, how do you train against something that there’s not a wide dataset for? It’s a big challenge.”

“We are providing robot safety simulation software that robotics companies or enterprises that are building robots can use to better provide evidence around safety, to test different types of safety scenarios before they happen in the real world, or test things that are effectively too rare, too dangerous, or too expensive to test in the real world,” he added.

Teams can build scenarios right in the browser from past incidents, safety standards, and robot logs, with no simulation expertise required. SafeWorld then runs the robot through thousands of variations with realistic, reactive human motion and measures safety performance.

Because every software update and new environment can introduce new risks, teams can rerun these tests continuously, not just once before launch. The result is a safety record that engineering, safety, and operations leaders can stand behind, claimed SafeWorld.

Wong noted that while many companies work with simulation, using it for safety brings new requirements.

“Where that breaks down and gets different is really in the nuance of the feature and functionality,” he said. “You have to figure out what even is the testing criteria for safety. You obviously have different standards, but those standards are not all complete. Then you have different types of risk assessments.”

When should companies start working with SafeWorld?

For some robotics developers, it can be hard to tell when it’s time to start investing in safety. If you start too early, your system may change significantly before seeing the real world, rendering much of your work useless. But, if you start too late, you run the risk of delaying deployments.

“We work with about half a dozen companies, and two-thirds of them are publicly traded companies,” Wong said. “I would say that if the timeline for your deployment is under one year, you probably need to start thinking about safety. If it’s beyond a year, it’s maybe a little too early.”

The question of when to start thinking about safety is also different depending on the type of company.

“There are two kinds of AI robotic companies. One is your bring AI to the robots. Another one, you bring robots to AI,” Wong said. The first category involves companies like Caterpillar, which already owns sophisticated hardware and wants to bring AI capabilities to that hardware.

For these customers, safety is important on Day 1, because they already have hardware out working in the world. If you’re starting with software, safety comes later when you start working in the real world, but getting ahead on safety can still help these companies streamline things later on.

“Safety has been foundational to Anyware Robotics from Day 1,” said Thomas Tang, CEO of Anyware Robotics. “Advanced simulation tools like SafeWorld give us a scalable way to test challenging scenarios, strengthen our safety processes, and better prepare our robots for real-world deployment.”

Register now and help us celebrate 20 years of RoboBusiness!

Startup plans to promote safety research

Looking ahead, SafeWorld said it plans to use its latest funding to deepen adoptions, build out its team, and promote safety research across the industry.

“We’re really trying to go super deep in terms of enterprise adoption and going super deep with some of our enterprise customers,” said Wong. “There’s so much to do here with safety, it makes sense for us to really focus on that delivery.”

“On the marketing side, we’re trying to do a lot in terms of promoting different research, whether that’s funding research or promoting research, and open-source work that is at the frontier of AI safety,” he added.

As the robotics industry grows, Ding and Wong agreed that having third parties like SafeWorld can help build trust with other stakeholders.

“Part of the reason why I think a third party is very helpful here is that there is an engineering part around safety, and then there is a trust part of safety, and you need both of those to deploy,” Wong said. “The trust part of safety is really around stakeholder management around safety and who actually signs off on that.”

“This is really a deployment problem. So, having a third-part company to work on this is really necessary to win trust not only for the company itself, but also for the whole industry,” Ding said.

item.title: Jabil discusses the pace of humanoid robot development and production
item.dc:creator: Eugene Demaitre
item.description:
Jabil, which is working with robot developers such as Apptronik, provides a design perspective on humanoid progress.

The post Jabil discusses the pace of humanoid robot development and production appeared first on The Robot Report.
item.ns3:encoded:
The Apollo humanoid robot is designed for a variety of applications. | Credit: Apptronik

While much of the focus on humanoid robots has been on entertaining demonstration videos and massive amounts of funds raised, the work of development and finding a value proposition is quietly continuing. How are humanoids progressing from prototypes to mass production? Jabil Inc., a design, supply chain, and manufacturing services provider, offered its perspective.

Companies preparing to ramp up production of humanoid robots include Tesla, 1X Technologies, XPeng, and UBTECH. Jabil works with robotics developers to bring their products to market at scale.

The St. Petersburg, Fla.-based company has worked with Apptronik on bringing its Apollo humanoid to active manufacturing environments. Thomas Brown, senior director for engineering and technology, including digital commerce and robotics, at Jabil, replied to the following questions from The Robot Report.

Setting realistic expectations for humanoid volume

How are investor and customer expectations for mobile manipulators and humanoids evolving?

Brown: In terms of managing expectations, a lot of customers have gotten humanoids out in low volumes, but we are entering a phase of tens of thousands, where it’s no longer something that’s assembled by hand on site. You’re starting to get to where you need a cost structure, manufacturability, and to improve quality. These are areas where Jabil can really add a lot of value.

When a robot’s much more expensive, there’s only so many they can produce for gathering AI training data, and they need more customer use-case validation. We provide that ability to cost down their designs to actually hit those scales.

How is the current boom in compute enabling more capable physical AI?

Brown: Compute is now sufficient for many of the experiences you see on the demo reels, but we do need more computing capacity at the edge. The NVIDIA Jetson series is a popular lineup for our customers developing their aspirations in the robotic space.

We’re getting more compute and memory, but prices are an ongoing pain point for scale. The foundation model makers are developing intelligence that’s outside that capacity, but expanding it is key.

We’ve seen Hyundai, Tesla, and BMW fund and test humanoids. What advantages do automotive partners bring to design for manufacturing?

Brown: Take wiring harnesses for humanoids. It needs a hybrid of automotive-type robustness with an extremely small form factor like high-grade consumer electronics.

Developers need to work with partners for rapid iteration. In addition to sensing and compute, there’s a wide range of power supplies, allowing for swapping.

What are some of the challenges in getting humanoids to market?

Brown: Prior to the smartphone, things were much more simplistic — you could just build up capabilities to the cost point and scale. Now, companies are resetting and diversifying their supply chains.

My company is working with major humanoid developers in the U.S. and abroad, but I can’t name them at this time.

Editor’s note: Physical AI and humanoids are among the session track topics at RoboBusiness 2026, which will be on Oct. 20 and 21 in Santa Clara, Calif. Register now to attend.

Register now and help us celebrate 20 years of RoboBusiness!

Where humanoids, mobile manipulators make sense

What is the commercial outlook for humanoids in factories and warehouses?

Brown: In manufacturing, there are a ton of spaces where humanoids make sense. When you look at a production line today, most automation is built for specific tasks, but the applicability of humanoids to a wide range of tasks changes the math from a purpose-built line.

A lot of these humanoid companies have done a good job of partnering with end customers to gather clear requirements. That’s a solid approach. In the consumer space, it’s still the science fiction route of “I just want a robot to fold laundry” or whatever the vague use case might be.

In terms of iterating, do humanoids need to equal human capabilities, or should developers be aiming for superhuman ability?

Brown: I think it’s more about having a super set of capabilities that you can apply in bits and pieces to other markets. You see it already with some of the humanoids, where they have a wheeled base instead of being bipedal. It’s a much easier problem to solve, and I would say that’s the same thing with having the fully embodied humanoid versus, say, one arm with the camera.

The company that conquers that can conquer all other challenges, but the company that conquers just one is going to struggle to go up the stack. You see many of these companies going after the larger play. Maybe some of them will completely hit it; maybe some of them won’t.

I would say it’s truly the super-set approach that they can decompose into specific solutions that are more cost-optimized, depending on the use case.

Do you see mobile manipulators as an interim step toward humanoids, or more of a standalone form factor?

Brown: I definitely think there’s a place for mobile arms. Even traditional automation like a machine tender running at 1.5 mps [3.3 mph] is pretty fast. A humanoid going that fast would be tremendously fast, let alone if it’s carrying a load.

There’s just different needs, depending on what the facility requires and what the existing line looks like. The humanoid is going to be a supremely flexible device, but it’s not always the right device. Traditional high-speed automation will still have a big play for the foreseeable future.

You had mentioned consumer robots, when and if do you think we can expect them?

Brown: Maybe in five-ish years. It could be 20 years, but progress is going very rapidly. If the model development continues at the pace it has and if the computing continues at the pace it has, we’re certainly going to be there on the AI and electronics hardware side.

There’s going to be a market for multiple humanoid companies because there’s so much diverse need. We’re talking manufacturing, consumer, hospitality, food prep. There’s so many different spaces to attack, and policy development in one area doesn’t mean you win in all the others.

There’s so many different levels of performance that you can put in the actuators that it creates a lot of possibilities for people who can fine-tune the solutions they want to go after. Even in our own factories, we’re going to have specific needs for automation, as we do today.

Both humanoid robots and the spaces around them will evolve

While humanoids are intended to fit into settings designed around humans, how could they affect factory and warehouse designs?

Brown: As humanoid robotic fleets become ubiquitous, they’ll change our assumptions on how we do line layout. If you’re able to define layout on the software, send work instructions, hit the “Go” button, execute, and have the humanoids pull out workstations, put on new end effectors for their arms, and pull supplies out of the back, that fundamentally changes how we look at manufacturing.

The lines are no longer the key limiting factor. It’s just about kind of your creativity, the robot fleet, almost like this programmable substrate for manufacturing, if you will. Along the way, we’re going to have more hybrid solutions, for sure.

In addition to developing explainable AI, what about the related concerns around humanoid safety?

Brown: For things like insurance, many robotic arms have safety certifications. There are norms for standoff distances, cages, etc. There’s a tremendous amount of infrastructure built around the end applications, so it’s going to take some time for the industry to get their hands around how humanoids operate.

What are their failure modes? How do we certify these things in new environments? How do we understand what the model is going to do in certain conditions? Yeah, there’s a tremendous amount of work that’s going to have to go into these systems to get them to a place to where we can truly rely on them like we can current automation solutions.

Companies are starting to track legislation and develop safety standards. Existing ones will have to be expanded to govern how these devices operate in commercial spaces, consumer space, and more.

I’m pretty optimistic about what the future holds. I see a lot of progress being made, and I think great things are in store for us. And I love working with our customers in this space, helping to bring those price points down and improve functionality.

item.title: Helm.ai reaches $70M in signed commercial contracts for its foundation models
item.dc:creator: Brianna Wessling
item.description:
Helm.ai trained its foundation models using its unsupervised 'deep teaching' methodology to master the structure of the physical world itself.

The post Helm.ai reaches $70M in signed commercial contracts for its foundation models appeared first on The Robot Report.
item.ns3:encoded:
Helm.ai said it has commercial partners spanning perception, full-stack autonomous driving, automated data labeling, and generative simulation. | Source: Helm.ai

Helm.ai today said it has signed $70 million in commercial contracts for its foundation models for physical AI over a 12-month period. These contracts spanned global automotive OEMs, Tier 1 suppliers, and industrial automation companies.

The Redwood City, Calif.-based company considers the automotive industry as its flagship deployments, which involve deep partnerships. But, it also has partnerships with customers in mining and construction.

“Those kinds of projects coming to that level of maturity are super exciting for us, because it demonstrates that there’s a real demand for the technology that we’ve built,” Vladislav Voroninski, founder and CEO of Helm.ai, told The Robot Report. “It’s clearly crossing that threshold into actually being deployed in the real world,”

“Also, as a company, we’re now on a path to break even, which is rare in this space, and it’s a testament to the capital efficiency of our approach,” he said.

Founded in 2016, Helm.ai’s software already spans SAE Level 2 through 4 autonomous vehicle (AV) programs, production-track perception in heavy industry, and expanding robotics development.

Inside Helm.ai’s ‘deep teaching’ methodology

Helm.ai trained its foundation models using its unsupervised “deep teaching” methodology to master the structure of the physical world itself. This separates the problem of understanding an environment from the problem of acting in it.

“The way we attack the problem is different from thinking about it as there’s some sensor data in, and a decision comes out,” Voroninski said. “We actually have structure throughout the stack, so each part of the stick is still learned end to end using DNNs [deep neural networks]. The way we think about solving the problem is, first, learn how to perceive the world, and then we actually act on that perception. So, it’s similar to how humans learn.”

Voroninski compared this to a teenager learning to drive. That teenager doesn’t have to drive for millions of hours to experience every single possible scenario they could encounter on the road.

“They can already perceive everything perfectly and make predictions about what the other vehicles or people might do, without actually relying on driving data,” said Voroninski. “That’s a pretty critical thing, and that gives us data efficiency, which is really important in the autonomous driving space, but it’s actually even more important in robotics. I would say it’s essential in robotics.”

An automaker simply has to figure out how they will ramp up collecting data. “For robotics applications, nobody has a large fleet of robots yet. There not really any data available to even train that way,” Voroninski said. “So, data efficiency becomes very, very important.”

“We factor our stack into perception, and then everything downstream from perception,” he continued. “That plays an important role in data efficiency as well as safety certification.”

The result is a system that learns from a fraction of the data, generalizes to environments it has never encountered, and deploys within the compute constraints of real-world physical systems, according to Helm.ai.

AVs give Helm.ai a foundation for scaling to different environments

Voroninski said an important aspect of Helm.ai’s technology is being environment-agnostic. The company’s roots are in autonomous driving, which already requires generalizing across a range of different environments. The system may have to handle a busy city street or a desert road. This provided a good foundation for generalizing across more environments, he pointed out.

“We’ve shown that our technology can generalize to entirely different application areas,” said Voroninski. “We can take the same perception stack and use it for autonomous driving purposes, an open pit mine, or other kinds of industrial environments.”

So far, Helm.ai has projects bound for production in AVs, mining, and construction. It has also applied its AI technology to delivery drones.

“When we train foundation models, we’re not just training on driving data or a specific target area,” Voroninski said. “Our foundation models are trained in a pretty general way across data sets that go well beyond those specific applications, and that’s similar to how a human would learn how to actually do these things.”

Helm.ai learned other things from the automotive industry. Autonomous driving comes with real-time latency constrains and rigorous safety regulations. Being able to handle that industry makes the company well equipped for others, Voroninski said.

Helm.ai’s software is robot-agnostic

Voroninski discussed using Helm.ai’s technology across autonomous vehicles, drones, humanoid robots, and more. While it may seem difficult to generalize to many robot form factors, Voroninski said these different form factors all come with similar problems.

“The perception problem starts with the sensors that you’re using and how they’re configured,” Voroninski said. For AVs, this typically means a 360º view with a camera stack, lidar, and radar.

“We’ve shown that we can work quite well with those types of sensor modalities and simulate all of those at the same time,” Voroninski said. “When you go to other domains, you’re still talking about sensors that are positioned on some form factor in some configuration. From that perspective, it’s exactly the same.”

“It’s essentially the same problem, just different definitions for what you want to detect, what you want to localize, and the kinds of behaviors you’re going to care about,” he continued.

A person on a construction site might behave differently from a pedestrian on the street. But, the same technology can make predictions about both of these people.

Looking ahead, Voroninski said Helm.ai is interested in working with robotics companies across industries and embodiments.

“Where robotics is now is almost where autonomous driving was 10 years ago,” Voroninski said. “It’s really now entering its breakout moment, so we’re just super excited to take things that we’ve learned from the commercial traction we’ve achieved, and apply that to many different areas.”
